{
  "reframes": [
    {
      "bottleneck": "The 1,000-member forecasts only reduce Monte-Carlo noise in the probability estimates of one learned distribution. If members really are exchangeable draws, the fair-CRPS/Brier gain from 50 to 1,000 members is fixed by sampling theory, so roughly $900 of the $963 buys a number predictable from ~200 members.",
      "assumption": "That the skill-versus-members curve must be measured with real 1,000-member forecasts, i.e., that members beyond ~50 carry new information rather than re-sampling the same afCRPS-trained distribution.",
      "reframe": "Reorder the steps: measure exchangeability first. Estimate pairwise member error correlation and effective ensemble size N_eff from a small pilot, derive the sampling-theory bound on the 50-to-1,000 skill gain, and validate the subsampling methodology for free on the existing 7,424-member HENS archive. Only run 1,000 members if measured correlation makes N_eff much smaller than N.",
      "question": "At leads of 1, 5 and 10 days, what is the mean pairwise error correlation rho among AIFS-ENS v1 members for 10 m wind, 2 m temperature and rain, and is the fair-CRPS gain predicted for 50 to 1,000 members, using N_eff = N/(1+(N-1)rho), larger than 1%?",
      "measure": "Run 100 members x 2 dates (~200 member-forecasts at ~$0.11 each, about $22, near the $19.90 check-first gate), compute pairwise member RMSE correlations per field and lead, derive N_eff and the beta-binomial sampling bound on Brier improvement; cross-check the skill-curve shape by subsampling the free HENS 7,424-member x 92-date archive on CPU.",
      "compute_after": "If members are near-iid, the 50-vs-1,000 question is settled for ~$25 and the remaining ~$900 buys more verifying dates, which is the real binding constraint on top-percentile skill confidence intervals. If rho is large, compute now buys diagnosis of a correlated-error structure the original design cannot even see.",
      "exact": "Mean pairwise member RMSE correlation rho for 10 m wind at day 5 across 100 members x 2 dates; N_eff(N) = N/(1+(N-1)rho); predicted Brier(1,000) minus Brier(50) from beta-binomial sampling of the event probabilities.",
      "expected": "rho small but positive (0.05-0.3); predicted 50-to-1,000 skill gain under 1-2%, i.e., saturation is largely a sampling identity, decided an order of magnitude cheaper than planned.",
      "fails_if": "A 200-vs-50-member subsample already beats the iid sampling bound, implying non-exchangeable structure (member drift or sub-populations) that only full 1,000-member runs can characterize.",
      "closest_prior": "HENS Part 2's 7,424-member tail sampling [s_hens]; the afCRPS paper's exchangeable-draws training claim [s_crps_paper]; classical effective-ensemble-size analysis (Leutbecher & Palmer 2008)."
    },
    {
      "bottleneck": "Estimating top-percentile probabilities by counting members makes cost scale linearly with tail rarity: the 99th percentile needs ~100 members, the 99.9th ~1,000, and each extra nine of rarity costs 10x the GPUs to sample the same unchanged distribution.",
      "assumption": "That the ensemble tail must be sampled empirically; that no cheaper estimator can extract more tail information per member.",
      "reframe": "Change the unit of work from member count to member-plus-tail-model: fit a generalized Pareto tail (peaks over threshold) to each grid point's 50-member ensemble and compare its exceedance probabilities against empirical counts from 200-1,000 members. If 50 fitted members match 1,000 raw members, member count stops being the compute axis.",
      "question": "Do GPD tails fitted to 50-member AIFS-ENS ensembles reproduce the top-1% exceedance-probability fields of a 1,000-member ensemble within the 1,000-member bootstrap sampling error, for 10 m wind, 2 m temperature and daily rain at days 5-10?",
      "measure": "Free methodology check on the existing HENS 7,424-member x 92-date archive: fit GPD to 50-member subsamples and score against the 7,424-member empirical tails (CPU-hours, under $5). Then one AIFS confirmation: 200 members x 1 date, about $22.",
      "compute_after": "If the tail model holds, every 50-member forecast yields 1,000-member-grade tail probabilities, so the same $963 buys roughly 20x more dates or variables, i.e., more independent extreme events to verify against, which is what actually limits rare-extreme skill estimates.",
      "exact": "Mean absolute error between 50-member GPD-fitted and 1,000-member empirical 99th-percentile exceedance probabilities over land grid points, compared against the 95% bootstrap band of the 1,000-member empirical estimate.",
      "expected": "Fitted tails within sampling noise at the 99th percentile, degrading near the 99.9th where even 1,000 members leave at most ~10 tail samples per grid point.",
      "fails_if": "The afCRPS-trained ensemble has bounded or light (shape xi < 0) tails, so GPD extrapolation biases exceedance probabilities beyond the fitted range and raw member count is genuinely the only route to rarer tails.",
      "closest_prior": "HENS Part 2's 4-sigma claims from raw 7,424-member counts [s_hens]; standard peaks-over-threshold/GPD extreme-value practice (Coles 2001); EVT-style tail extension behind products like ECMWF's EFI."
    },
    {
      "bottleneck": "The hypothesized cap is error shared by all members, yet the design varies only member count within one trained distribution: it can detect a plateau but cannot spend its way past it, so at saturation each extra GPU-hour provably buys more of the same.",
      "assumption": "That the single AIFS-ENS v1 weight set must be held fixed; that an ensemble means draws of one distribution rather than a choice of how many distinct error modes to sample per dollar.",
      "reframe": "Hold GPU-hours fixed and make diversity the axis: K error-decorrelated ensembles (different training checkpoints or seeds of the afCRPS run, or AIFS-ENS pooled with another ML ensemble) with N/K members each, versus N members of the single model. Score top-percentile Brier and fair CRPS at equal cost.",
      "question": "At equal GPU-hours, does pooling 5 training checkpoints x 200 members beat 1,000 members of the single AIFS-ENS v1 distribution on top-1% 10 m-wind Brier score, i.e., does between-checkpoint error decorrelation exceed the within-ensemble sampling gain?",
      "measure": "Pilot: 3 checkpoints x 100 members x 1 date (~300 member-forecasts, about $33; checkpoints already exist from training, inference only). Measure the top-1% wind Brier of the pooled 300-member ensemble versus 300 members of the reference checkpoint, plus the between-checkpoint day-5 RMSE correlation as the diversity diagnostic.",
      "compute_after": "If diversity wins, more compute buys additional independent error modes, so skill can keep rising exactly where the single-model curve was flat, and the design directly tests the root question's shared-error cap instead of only observing a plateau. If pooling 3 checkpoints gains nothing, the shared-error cap is confirmed early and cheaply.",
      "exact": "Difference in top-1% 10 m-wind Brier score between (a) 300 members pooled across 3 checkpoints and (b) 300 members of the reference checkpoint on one shared date, with between-checkpoint 10 m-wind error correlation at days 1, 5 and 10.",
      "expected": "Checkpoints from one training run show high day-5 error correlation and pooling gains little, confirming shared error dominates; any measurable decorrelation reopens the skill curve at fixed budget.",
      "fails_if": "Only one usable checkpoint exists, or between-checkpoint error correlation exceeds 0.99 at all leads, so the diversity axis buys nothing and the single-distribution design stands.",
      "closest_prior": "Multi-model versus single-model ensemble comparisons showing diversity beats size at fixed cost (TIGGE/ENSEMBLES-era results; Leutbecher & Palmer 2008); HENS [s_hens] as the single-model large-N reference point."
    }
  ]
}
